paragraphs: Learning directly on a device could reduce communication delays, limit privacy risks from exchanging information with servers, and improve energy efficiency. The obstacle is that training requires memory and computation that small devices may struggle to provide. This paper focuses on activation memory, a bottleneck associated with the intermediate information used during backpropagation.

Earlier approaches have addressed this bottleneck through low-rank decomposition. The authors propose a shortcut approach as an alternative and examine it through both analysis and experiments. Its importance lies in targeting two resource demands together: the memory occupied by activations and the arithmetic work required for training.

On the traditional benchmarks evaluated, the method reduces activation memory by up to a factor of 120.09 relative to vanilla training, while reducing overall training FLOPs by up to a factor of 1.86. These are reported maximum improvements, rather than savings promised for every setting. The findings support shortcuts as a potentially useful route toward making on-device training more practical.
icml-2025-beyond-low-rank-decomposition-.tldr: A shortcut approach reduces activation memory and training computation, with large reported savings on benchmarks relevant to on-device learning.

paragraphs: Group distributionally robust optimization seeks parameters that perform well against the group with the highest risk. Worst-case sample requirements can grow with the total number of groups, K. This paper asks whether fewer samples suffice when only a small subset of groups has substantially higher risk at any given parameter setting.

The authors formalize this structure through a sparsity condition: at each parameter setting, at most beta groups have risks separated from all remaining groups by a margin of at least lambda. Under this condition, their algorithm replaces dependence on K with dependence on beta in the accuracy-dependent part of sample complexity. The analysis connects the optimization problem to sleeping bandits and their guarantees for individual actions.

An adaptive algorithm adjusts to the best applicable sparsity condition, up to logarithmic factors. The paper also provides a computationally efficient, semi-adaptive method with a dimension-free bound. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets support the condition’s practical relevance and show improved sample efficiency. The benefit therefore comes from exploitable group-risk structure rather than an unconditional improvement for every problem.
icml-2025-beyond-minimax-rates-in-group-.tldr: When relatively few groups have distinctly high risk, group-robust optimization can reduce its accuracy-dependent sample requirements.

paragraphs: DCTdiff studies image generation using frequency information represented by the discrete cosine transform. Its diffusion model operates in this transformed space, making the choice of image representation central to the generation process. The paper develops an end-to-end approach and investigates which design choices make it work effectively.

Experiments span the UViT and DiT frameworks, different generation tasks, and multiple diffusion samplers. Across these evaluations, the authors report better image quality and training efficiency than pixel-based diffusion models. They also demonstrate generation at 512-by-512 resolution without a latent diffusion pipeline, outperforming the evaluated latent diffusion setup using SD-VAE at one-quarter of its training cost.

The paper connects these practical results to a theoretical interpretation of diffusion. It proves a relationship under which image diffusion can be understood as spectral autoregression, linking diffusion to autoregressive modeling through frequency structure. Together, the experiments and analysis suggest that frequency-space representations can improve generation efficiency while offering a useful perspective on how diffusion constructs images.
icml-2025-dctdiff-intriguing-properties-.tldr: DCTdiff generates images in frequency space, improving reported quality and training efficiency while connecting diffusion to spectral autoregression.

paragraphs: A finished poster combines visual elements into one image, but precise editing benefits from recovering those elements as separate layers. This paper introduces a task that converts composite graphic designs into ordered layers containing color and transparency, together with descriptive metadata. Such a representation supports editing, managing, and reusing individual parts of a design.

The task requires identifying each layer’s attributes and reconstructing portions hidden behind overlapping elements. The proposed Decompose Layer Model, or DeaM, combines a visual encoder, a language model, and a decoder that generates color and transparency conditioned on layer information. Processing happens in two stages: generating layer metadata, including spatial coordinates and quantized encodings, then reconstructing the corresponding layer images.

DeaM also supports interactive decomposition through text or point prompts, allowing users to guide the process. The experiments demonstrate the method’s effectiveness. The contribution is a unified approach to recovering both the structure of a graphic design and the visual content needed to make that structure useful for subsequent editing.
icml-2025-decomposition-of-graphic-desig.tldr: DeaM turns composite graphic designs into editable layers and metadata, including reconstruction of regions hidden by overlap.

paragraphs: An effective decision-maker must sometimes choose an action to learn about its consequences, rather than simply select the option that currently looks best. EVOLvE investigates how well language models perform this exploration in bandit problems, a reinforcement learning setting without evolving states. Its evaluation suite includes both context-free and contextual tasks at different difficulty levels.

The authors use knowledge from exploration algorithms to improve language-model decisions. One approach supplies explicit algorithmic guidance during inference. Another transfers algorithm behavior through demonstrations in the prompt or fine-tuning on synthetic examples generated by those algorithms. These routes test whether established decision rules can strengthen exploration without relying only on model scale.

The techniques enable smaller models to outperform larger models on various evaluated tasks. Additional experiments examine how difficulty and data representation influence exploration efficiency. A regret-based analysis links exploration performance to model size and the underlying algorithm. Together, these results show that incorporating algorithmic knowledge can materially improve the decision-making behavior measured by this benchmark.
icml-2025-evolve-evaluating-and-optimizi.tldr: EVOLvE benchmarks language-model exploration and shows that algorithmic guidance can help smaller models outperform larger ones.

paragraphs: Finding an equilibrium in a game does not settle which equilibrium is most desirable when several exist. This paper focuses on steering learning toward equilibria with higher welfare. It works within Policy Space Response Oracles, or PSRO, a framework that repeatedly expands an empirical game using strategies learned through deep reinforcement learning.

The proposed Ex²PSRO method changes how new strategies are explored. At each iteration, it builds an exploration policy by imitating behavior that produces high welfare. It then trains a response to the current game solution while regularizing that response to resemble the exploration policy. This introduces a preference for desirable outcomes during strategy discovery.

In a sequential bargaining game and a social dilemma game, Ex²PSRO tends to find higher-welfare equilibria than vanilla PSRO without additional simulation expense. Further experiments show that it can be combined with other PSRO variants and that the choice of exploration policy affects performance. The results support welfare-directed exploration as a practical influence on equilibrium selection in the tested settings.
icml-2025-explicit-exploration-for-high-.tldr: Ex²PSRO steers strategy exploration toward higher welfare and tends to find better-welfare equilibria without extra simulation expense.

paragraphs: FactTest treats the decision to trust a language-model answer as a statistical testing problem. Its central concern is falsely accepting hallucinated content as truthful. The framework allows a user to specify a significance level and provides a high-probability guarantee controlling this error, giving factuality assessment a formal statistical target.

The method is distribution-free and can operate with any number of human-annotated samples. It is also model-agnostic, covering language models whose internals are accessible as well as black-box systems. Beyond controlling false acceptance, the authors prove control of the opposite error under mild conditions and describe an extension for settings where the input distribution shifts.

On question-answering benchmarks, FactTest detects hallucinations and supports abstention when the model cannot answer reliably. The experiments report an accuracy improvement exceeding 40%. This finding concerns a system that can decline questions, alongside its statistical testing guarantees; the framework’s contribution is to connect that practical behavior with explicit control over specified factuality errors.
icml-2025-facttest-factuality-testing-in.tldr: FactTest uses statistical testing to control false acceptance of hallucinations and support language-model abstention.

paragraphs: Global minimum cut is a graph optimization problem that is often solved repeatedly on related instances. Standard practice starts each solve from scratch, leaving information from previous instances unused. This paper investigates how predictions informed by earlier problems can provide a useful starting point for established minimum-cut algorithms.

The authors adapt Karger’s algorithm and the Karger-Stein algorithm, both of which use randomized edge contraction. Their guiding idea is to change the contraction probabilities so that edges predicted to be outside the minimum cut are more likely to be contracted. Predictions therefore influence the existing search process through decisions about which edges to collapse.

With good predictions, the adapted algorithms achieve near-linear running time. The authors also show robustness to incorrect predictions, addressing the possibility that guidance from prior instances may be imperfect. The result identifies a way to exploit repetition across related optimization problems while retaining randomized contraction as the underlying algorithmic approach. The strongest speed guarantee is explicitly conditional on prediction quality.
icml-2025-faster-global-minimum-cut-with.tldr: Predictions guide randomized minimum-cut algorithms toward near-linear running time when accurate, with robustness to prediction errors.

paragraphs: Multimodal information often forms a network of relationships more complex than individual image-caption pairs. Images and text can share references and contextual connections both within and across modalities. Graph4MM investigates how these connections can directly shape multimodal learning, addressing approaches that treat graph structure as a separate input modality or fail to distinguish neighbors at different distances.

The framework introduces Hop-Diffused Attention, which incorporates information from multiple graph hops into self-attention using causal masking and hop diffusion. It also introduces MM-QFormer, a querying transformer designed to fuse information across modalities through multiple mappings. Together, these components address structural integration and the combination of modality-specific content.

Theoretical and empirical analyses support using graph relationships to organize interactions within and between modalities. Across generative and discriminative tasks, Graph4MM outperforms the evaluated larger vision-language models, language models, and multimodal graph baselines, with a reported average improvement of 6.93%. The findings indicate that exploiting relationships among inputs can improve multimodal understanding beyond simply supplying graph information as another modality.
icml-2025-graph4mm-weaving-multimodal-le.tldr: Graph4MM integrates graph relationships into attention and cross-modal fusion, improving performance on evaluated multimodal tasks.

paragraphs: Latent action learning aims to extract action-like representations from observations without requiring action labels throughout pre-training. That makes video a potentially valuable resource for embodied AI. This paper examines a complication: real videos contain distracting changes correlated with actions, whereas earlier work mainly studied observations whose changes were explained by the actual actions.

Using the Distracting Control Suite, the authors show empirically that Latent Action Policies, or LAPO, struggle with these distractors. They introduce LAOM, a simple modification that improves latent-action quality eightfold according to linear probing. This evaluates the learned representation separately from its eventual use in a downstream task.

The authors also provide ground-truth action supervision during representation learning. With labels for as little as 2.5% of the full dataset, downstream performance improves by 4.2 times on average. These findings suggest that early supervision can be critical when distractors are present. They challenge the conventional sequence of first learning latent actions without labels and only afterward learning how those representations correspond to real actions.
icml-2025-latent-action-learning-require.tldr: Experiments with distractors show that small amounts of action supervision during latent-action learning can substantially improve downstream performance.

paragraphs: Neural-network layers differ in dimensions, activation functions, structure, and the representations they learn. These differences also evolve during training. This paper develops a quantization framework that adapts to such layer-level variation, rather than treating the information handled by every layer as interchangeable.

The framework provides tight bounds on quantization variance and code length. These quantities describe two connected concerns: the variability introduced by quantization and the length of its encoded representation. The authors then apply a new layer-wise technique to distributed variational inequalities, introducing Quantized Optimistic Dual Averaging, or QODA, with adaptive learning rates.

For monotone variational inequalities, QODA achieves competitive convergence rates. Its practical evaluation trains a Wasserstein GAN using more than twelve GPUs and reports up to a 150% speedup over the baselines in end-to-end training time. The theoretical result is tied to the monotone setting, while the speedup is an empirical result from the evaluated training setup. Together, they connect adaptive layer-wise compression with both optimization analysis and measured training efficiency.
icml-2025-layer-wise-quantization-for-qu.tldr: QODA combines adaptive layer-wise quantization with distributed optimization, providing convergence results and reported multi-GPU training speedups.

paragraphs: Training large networks consumes memory for the optimizer’s internal state as well as model parameters. This paper introduces two complementary ways to reduce that state while accelerating learning. Subset-Norm shares step sizes among parameter subsets, generalizing AdaGrad variants and reducing the stated memory requirement from order d to order square root of d, where d is model size.

Subspace-Momentum stores momentum only in a low-dimensional subspace and uses stochastic gradient descent in the orthogonal complement. The authors prove high-probability convergence rates for this technique under standard assumptions. For Subset-Norm, they establish a noise-adapted guarantee with improved dimensional dependence for smooth non-convex objectives under coordinate-wise sub-Gaussian noise.

Experiments cover language-model pre-training and fine-tuning. Combining both techniques matches Adam’s validation perplexity on LLaMA 1B after 6.8 billion training tokens, compared with 13.1 billion for Adam. It also reduces optimizer-state memory by more than 80%, with minimal extra hyperparameter tuning. This example demonstrates that substantial state compression can coexist with improved token efficiency in the evaluated setting.
icml-2025-lean-and-mean-adaptive-optimiz.tldr: Sharing step sizes and restricting momentum reduces optimizer memory and matches Adam’s perplexity with roughly half the tokens in a reported LLaMA experiment.

paragraphs: Comparing datasets becomes difficult when they have different numbers of classes or entirely different labels. This paper introduces sliced optimal transport dataset distance, or s-OTDD, to compare datasets without training a model or requiring a particular model or embedding. The approach incorporates labels through the feature distributions associated with them.

Its central mechanism, Moment Transform Projection, converts a label represented by a feature distribution into a real number. Combined with a data-point projection, this turns each dataset into a one-dimensional distribution. The distance averages Wasserstein distances between these projected distributions over random projection parameters, using the closed-form solution available for one-dimensional optimal transport.

The resulting computation is near-linear in data-point count and feature dimensionality, with no dependence on the number of classes. The authors report strong correlation with optimal transport dataset distance and greater efficiency than existing discrepancy measures. It also correlates with transfer-learning performance gaps and classification accuracy under data augmentation, suggesting practical value for assessing dataset relationships without training a comparison model.
icml-2025-lightspeed-geometric-dataset-d.tldr: s-OTDD efficiently compares datasets through one-dimensional projections that preserve information about features and label distributions.

paragraphs: MUFFIN is a neural audio-compression framework designed to preserve perceptual quality across different kinds of sound. Its approach uses psychoacoustic guidance to reconstruct multiple frequency bands, making the allocation of compressed information sensitive to how sound is perceived. The goal is efficient compression that retains the details important to listening quality.

The central mechanism quantizes latent speech representations across frequency bands using multi-band spectral residual vector quantization. Separate codebooks distinguish content from speaker attributes, while band-specific processing supports bitrate allocation. A fully convolutional architecture, inspired by transformers and equipped with modified snake activation functions, aims to capture fine frequency details more precisely.

Evaluations on LibriTTS, IEMOCAP, GTZAN, and BBC report consistently stronger reconstruction performance across the tested domains. The authors also report a high-compression variant that preserves reconstruction quality and strong results on downstream generative tasks. These findings suggest that MUFFIN’s compressed representations may be useful both for audio reconstruction and as tokens for integration with large language models.
icml-2025-multi-band-frequency-reconstru.tldr: MUFFIN uses perceptually guided frequency-band compression to improve audio reconstruction and provide useful representations for generative tasks.

paragraphs: Linear attention offers linear inference time and fixed memory usage, but training competitive language models with it from scratch is expensive. MVA instead converts pretrained Softmax-attention models. The aim is to retain the capabilities already learned while gaining the computational properties of linear attention.

The paper unifies several linear-attention methods through high-order query-key integration and multi-level vocabulary decomposition. The first explains combinations of linear and sparse attention in terms of collecting information across frequency bands. The second recursively uses information lost during state compression to expand memory capacity. Error analysis supports a better approximation to Softmax attention, and a soft integration strategy combines attention scores with a sliding window.

With fewer than 100 million fine-tuning tokens, the method reaches linear complexity while retaining a reported 99% of original performance. It improves MMLU by 1.2 percentage points over the compared state-of-the-art linear-attention model and method. Without the sliding window, it also reports state-of-the-art results across all evaluated test sets after 10 billion tokens, providing evidence for the underlying conversion approach.
icml-2025-mva-linear-attention-with-high.tldr: MVA converts pretrained language models to linear attention while retaining most reported performance with limited fine-tuning.

paragraphs: This paper studies learning in environments where an opponent strategically adapts over time. It models the interaction as a Markov game and focuses on policy regret, making the learner’s performance under an adaptive opponent the central concern. The setting extends beyond problems represented by explicit tables to larger problems handled through function approximation.

The authors propose a general algorithmic framework with an optimal regret rate of order square root of T. The guarantee applies to a broad class of problems satisfying an Eluder-type condition. That qualification matters: the result establishes a rate for a characterized problem class, rather than claiming that all games with adaptive opponents admit the same guarantee.

The framework also reveals a simpler algorithmic approach for reactive adversaries. Its key insight is to exploit the opponent’s learning behavior when choosing how to act. The contribution therefore combines a stronger reach beyond earlier tabular settings with an explanation of what enables the optimal rate: accounting for how the opponent learns within the evolving interaction.
icml-2025-policy-regret-minimization-in-.tldr: A framework exploiting opponent learning achieves optimal square-root policy regret for a broad, conditionally characterized class of Markov games.

paragraphs: Few-shot image classification has very little labeled real data available for training. Synthetic images can increase the training supply, but differences between synthetic and real distributions can also hurt performance. This paper develops a theoretical framework for understanding how those discrepancies affect supervised image classification.

The framework is intended to guide both the generation of useful synthetic samples and the training of a predictor that generalizes well. Building on it, the authors introduce an algorithm that incorporates prototype learning and jointly addresses data partitioning and model training. This connects the way real and synthetic data are organized with the way the classifier learns from them.

Experiments across multiple datasets report better performance than the compared state-of-the-art approaches. The findings support treating synthetic-data augmentation as a distribution-alignment problem, rather than assuming additional generated examples will automatically help. The paper’s contribution joins a theoretical account of the real–synthetic gap with a concrete learning procedure designed to reduce its effect in few-shot classification.
icml-2025-provably-improving-generalizat.tldr: A theory-guided prototype-learning method improves few-shot classification by addressing distribution differences between real and synthetic data.

paragraphs: Knowledge editing changes model weights to update particular factual associations. Such edits can also damage broader recall and reasoning, but performance measurements alone do not explain why. This paper constructs a synthetic task to examine that mechanism in a Transformer trained from scratch on a structured knowledge graph.

The graph links facts so that changing one association has implications for other entities. This makes it possible to inspect whether an edit preserves the relationships needed for additional inferences. The evaluations show that editing can alter representations beyond the intended entity and distort the structure supporting inference about knowledge the model has not directly seen.

The authors call this phenomenon representation shattering and demonstrate that it harms factual recall and reasoning on the task. They also corroborate the findings in more naturalistic settings with pretrained Llama and Mamba models. The result is a mechanistic hypothesis for editing failures: targeted weight changes can disrupt shared representational relationships that support capabilities beyond the fact being edited.
icml-2025-representation-shattering-in-t.tldr: Knowledge edits can distort representations of related entities, offering a mechanistic explanation for damage to recall and reasoning.

paragraphs: Multimodal models should adjust how much they rely on each modality as input quality changes from sample to sample. Attention mechanisms are designed to enable this flexibility. Through controlled experiments, this paper finds that widely used self-attention models can lose that adaptability and favor one modality regardless of the current input.

The authors identify a self-reinforcing process: preference for one modality increases its dominance, while attention-key distributions across modalities move further apart. This weakens attention’s ability to shift emphasis dynamically. Rolling Query, or RollingQ, addresses the process by rotating the query to balance attention allocation and reduce the gap between key distributions.

Experiments across multiple multimodal scenarios validate the method’s effectiveness and support the importance of restoring cooperation among modalities. The contribution combines a diagnosis of how adaptive fusion can deteriorate with a targeted intervention in the attention mechanism. Its practical significance is that having attention available does not by itself ensure input-sensitive fusion; the learned dynamics must also preserve that flexibility.
icml-2025-rollingq-reviving-the-cooperat.tldr: RollingQ rotates attention queries to counter self-reinforcing modality bias and restore adaptive multimodal fusion.

paragraphs: Synthetic text could support useful language-model fine-tuning while protecting real training examples, but combining readable text with formal guarantees is difficult. This paper proposes a theoretically grounded generation method that targets convergence, task performance, and privacy together. Its objective is to preserve the learning effect of real data in generated text.

The method uses the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers to iteratively optimize synthetic-example embeddings. It matches them to a noisy gradient computed from target training or validation data, then maps the optimized representations into token sequences with low perplexity. This connects the synthetic examples to the model updates induced by the target data while also encouraging readable output.

The authors guarantee convergence to a close neighborhood of the solution obtained by fine-tuning on real data, together with privacy preservation. The guarantee concerns proximity to that solution, rather than exact equality. Experiments on several classification tasks confirm the approach’s effectiveness, supporting gradient matching as a principled way to generate training text with both optimization and privacy objectives.
icml-2025-synthetic-text-generation-for-.tldr: Gradient matching generates readable synthetic text with privacy guarantees and convergence near the solution obtained from real-data fine-tuning.

paragraphs: A jailbreak can make a language model answer a prohibited question, but that does not establish whether the answer is useful or correct. This paper separates those outcomes. It studies whether bypassing refusal also reduces the quality of the resulting response, calling the observed loss in utility the jailbreak tax.

To make answer quality rigorously measurable, the authors align models to refuse benign topics with known answers, such as mathematics or biology. They then evaluate eight representative jailbreaks across five utility benchmarks. This setup allows them to measure correctness after refusal is bypassed without needing to judge the practical effectiveness of dangerous instructions.

The evaluations show a consistent utility drop in jailbroken responses. All tested jailbreaks bypass the math-refusal guardrails, yet accuracy falls by as much as 92%. These results establish that successful bypass and useful output can diverge sharply in the studied settings. The paper introduces benchmarks and proposes output utility as an additional metric for evaluating jailbreaks.
icml-2025-the-jailbreak-tax-how-useful-a.tldr: Jailbreaks that successfully bypass refusals can substantially reduce answer correctness, motivating a separate measure of output utility.

paragraphs: Federated learning keeps clients’ raw data from being directly shared with a coordinating server, but this alone does not settle privacy questions. Membership inference attacks seek to determine whether particular data participated in training. This paper examines such attacks when clients also use local differential privacy, explicitly incorporating that protection into the analysis.

The authors derive lower bounds on the success rates of low-polynomial-time attacks exploiting fully connected or self-attention layers. Their bounds apply regardless of which local differential privacy mechanism is used. The resulting privacy risk depends on the privacy budget, so the analysis characterizes residual exposure under protection rather than treating privacy as simply present or absent.

Evaluations with models including ResNet and Vision Transformer confirm considerable risks in the studied settings. They also show that increasing noise enough to mitigate these attacks significantly harms model utility. The contribution connects theoretical attack-success guarantees with a practical privacy–utility tradeoff, clarifying why protected federated training can still permit meaningful membership inference.
icml-2025-theoretically-unmasking-infere.tldr: Theoretical bounds and vision-model experiments show privacy-budget-dependent membership risks even with local differential privacy.

paragraphs: A world model used for control must predict changes over time, and the interval between observations affects the dynamics it needs to capture. The Time-Aware World Model makes that interval an explicit input. It conditions predictions on the time-step size and trains across a range of intervals instead of using one fixed sampling interval.

This design allows the model to learn both high-frequency and low-frequency task dynamics. Its motivation is information-theoretic: the most suitable sampling rate depends on the system’s underlying behavior. Making elapsed time part of the formulation gives the model a direct way to account for that relationship across different control problems.

Empirical evaluations report consistently better performance than conventional models across varying observation rates and multiple control tasks. The comparisons use the same numbers of training samples and iterations. These findings support the claim that explicitly modeling time-step size can improve performance and data efficiency, showing value from the formulation itself within the evaluated training budgets.
icml-2025-time-aware-world-model-for-ada.tldr: Conditioning a world model on elapsed time improves prediction and control across varying observation rates in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Spiking neural networks are being explored as a response to the energy demands of conventional neural networks, but their theoretical foundations are less developed. This paper studies a widely used discrete-time formulation built from leaky integrate-and-fire neurons. Its focus is what functions these networks can represent and how their architecture affects that ability.

The authors show that these networks produce piecewise constant functions over polyhedral regions of the input space. In plain terms, inputs are divided into geometrically defined regions, with a constant output within each region. They also quantify the network size needed to approximate continuous functions, connecting this representational structure to approximation capability.

The analysis examines both latency, measured in time steps, and depth, measured in layers. It shows the importance of latency for the complexity of the induced input partition and contrasts these networks with conventional networks using piecewise linear activations. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings, giving a clearer account of how time and depth shape the studied spiking networks.
icml-2025-time-to-spike-understanding-th.tldr: The paper characterizes discrete-time spiking networks’ representational power and shows how latency and depth shape their input partitions.

paragraphs: This paper seeks a mechanism explaining how diffusion models generalize. The authors compare pretrained diffusion networks with theoretically optimal empirical counterparts and identify a shared preference for local operations across several network architectures. That observation motivates their hypothesis that localized denoising is a central part of the networks’ generalization behavior.

The proposed explanation is that local denoising approximates the training objective well over much of the training distribution. To test this idea, the authors construct training-free algorithms that aggregate local empirical denoisers. These algorithms provide a concrete way to ask whether the proposed mechanism can reproduce the behavior of trained network denoisers.

Comparisons cover both forward and reverse diffusion processes. The constructed algorithms produce outputs with consistent visual similarity to network outputs and lower mean squared error than previously proposed explanatory methods. This agreement supports localized denoising as a mechanistic hypothesis. The contribution is both an explanation grounded in observed network behavior and a set of algorithms that make the explanation experimentally testable.
icml-2025-towards-a-mechanistic-explanat.tldr: Training-free local denoisers reproduce aspects of diffusion-network behavior, supporting a localized-denoising explanation of generalization.
